title: Superposition
kicker: A qubit is not secretly 0 or 1. It carries two amplitudes at once.
summary: A qubit's state is a weighted combination of |0⟩ and |1⟩. The weights are amplitudes: complex numbers whose squared sizes give the chances of measuring 0 or 1. Superposition is what lets amplitudes add up or cancel, which is where every quantum speedup starts.

blocks.heading: Two amplitudes, not two values
blocks.body:
A classical bit is either 0 or 1. A qubit's state is written |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are complex numbers called *amplitudes*.

When you measure the qubit you get 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². Because one of the two must happen, the amplitudes always satisfy |α|² + |β|² = 1.

blocks.caption: Any single-qubit state. Measuring gives 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|².

blocks.title: An equal superposition
blocks.caption: The Hadamard gate takes |0⟩ to (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2: each outcome now has amplitude 1/√2, so probability ½.

blocks.heading: Why it is not just a coin flip
blocks.body:
A 50/50 superposition and a fair coin give the same statistics if you measure straight away. The difference shows up when you act on the qubit first.

Apply a second Hadamard. The two paths that lead to |1⟩ have amplitudes +½ and −½ and cancel; the two paths to |0⟩ add to 1. The qubit returns to |0⟩ with certainty. A randomly set coin cannot do that. This cancelling and reinforcing is *interference*.

blocks.title: Interference: H twice
blocks.caption: The amplitudes for |1⟩ cancel and those for |0⟩ add, so the second Hadamard undoes the first.

ops.note: The |1⟩ amplitudes cancel; the qubit is back to |0⟩.

blocks.title: An unequal superposition
blocks.caption: A rotation RY(π/3) gives amplitudes cos(π/6) ≈ 0.866 and sin(π/6) = 0.5, so probabilities ¾ and ¼.

ops.note: Rotate by π/3 about the Y axis.

blocks.myth: A qubit in superposition is really 0 or 1; we just don't know which yet.
blocks.truth: If that were true, applying H twice could not return |0⟩ every time. A hidden 0 or 1 would come out of two Hadamards as 0 or 1 with equal odds. The exact return to |0⟩ is interference between amplitudes, which a hidden definite value cannot produce.

blocks.myth: Superposition means a quantum computer tries every answer at once and reads them all out.
blocks.truth: A measurement returns one outcome. An algorithm must arrange interference so that wrong answers cancel and right ones reinforce before measuring. Superposition alone gives no speedup.

blocks.question: The qubit starts in |1⟩ and you apply a Hadamard. What are the probabilities of measuring 0 and 1, and how does the state differ from H|0⟩?
blocks.answer: Both probabilities are ½, exactly as for H|0⟩. The difference is the sign of the |1⟩ amplitude, a phase of π. It does not change these probabilities, but it changes what happens after further gates: H(H|1⟩) returns |1⟩, not |0⟩.

sources.title: M. A. Nielsen and I. L. Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (10th anniversary ed., Cambridge University Press, 2010), ch. 1
